Book 19 of the Analects, 子張 Zǐ zhāng, named, as every book is, from its first words — the disciple Zizhang, whose saying opens it. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 19 has 25 passages, and the Master speaks in none of them except at second hand: Zhu Xi says the whole book records the sayings of disciples, Zixia's the most and Zigong's next, since after Yan Hui none was quicker to understand than Zigong and after Master Zeng none more solid than Zixia. Zizhang opens with what makes an officer — ready to give his life in danger, thinking of what is right when gain is in sight — and with the man who holds virtue too narrowly to count either way (19.1–2); asked by Zixia's pupils about keeping company, he sets a broader rule against their teacher's (19.3). Zixia's sayings follow: small ways not to be followed far, learning day by day what one lacks, learning broadly and thinking of what is near, the craftsman in his workshop and the gentleman in his learning, the small man who dresses up his faults, the gentleman's three changes of aspect, winning trust before putting people to work or remonstrating, great virtue and small (19.4–11). Ziyou mocks Zixia's pupils as drilled in sweeping and answering but without the root, and Zixia answers that the Way is taught in order, as plants are told apart by kinds (19.12); then comes his pairing of office and learning (19.13). Ziyou and Master Zeng speak on mourning and on Zizhang, who aims too high (19.14–16); Master Zeng reports two sayings of the Master, on mourning for a parent and on Meng Zhuangzi, who kept his father's ministers and government (19.17–18), and tells a new officer of justice to pity the guilty, not to rejoice in finding them out (19.19). The last six passages are Zigong's: Zhou, the last Shang king, was not as wicked as his name, and that is why the gentleman will not live low down the stream, where all the world's bad things end up (19.20); the gentleman's faults are seen by all, like an eclipse, and so is his mending of them (19.21); the Master learned wherever the Way of the founding kings lived on among men (19.22); and to men who rated Zigong above the Master, or ran the Master down, he answers with a shoulder-high wall against one several times a man's height, hills against the sun and moon, and a Heaven no stair can climb (19.23–25). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.
